findings.current_title: Finalize-versus-child-write interleaving — unreachable: finalization is permanently retired and cannot be invoked by any runtime role
findings.affected_roles: None reachable. anon, authenticated and service_role all lack EXECUTE on finalize_session and are NOLOGIN; only the table owner/postgres could still invoke it, and the flag CHECK plus the transition trigger would still refuse the write.
findings.exact_current_source: supabase/migrations/0159_retire_signed_clinical_records.sql:175-183 (`revoke all on function public.finalize_session(uuid, integer) from public, anon, authenticated, service_role` plus the three correction/amendment RPCs); :190-191 (build_session_snapshot revoked from service_role too); :203-212 (all five _apply_*_correction appliers revoked); :151-161 (studios_clinical_finalization_retired / studios_clinical_corrections_retired CHECK constraints pin both flags false); :241-277 (guard_retired_finalization_transition + sessions_guard_retired_finalization trigger refuse any transition of record_status into 'finalized'/'void' and any non-'draft' INSERT); :287-317 (guard_retired_signed_ledger_insert blocks INSERT on clinical_record_snapshots, clinical_record_amendments, clinical_audit_events). Caller trace: repo-wide grep across app, lib and components for finalize_session / correct_finalized_session / amend_finalized_session / build_session_snapshot / clinical_finalization_enabled returns only lib/types/database.ts:35,38 (optional type fields) — there is no server action, route handler or component that calls the finalizer. The only remaining runtime read of the lifecycle column is app/(app)/clients/[id]/sessions/[sessionId]/page.tsx:299, which merely derives a read-only flag from `record_status === "finalized" || record_status === "void"`. The lock-order hazard the audit's fix would have introduced is documented at 0159:109-117 (a session-level FOR UPDATE inside a charting path deadlocks 40P01 against soft_delete_session_area; FOR NO KEY UPDATE is the compatible mode).
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: Hosted facts (authoritative, supplied): EXECUTE is revoked from public/anon/authenticated/service_role on all 10 retired functions including finalize_session and build_session_snapshot; both studio flags are FALSE on all 5 studios and pinned by two VALIDATED CHECK constraints; a transition guard refuses record_status moving into finalized/void; INSERT is blocked on all three signed ledgers; Willow has ZERO non-draft sessions; there is exactly ONE legacy finalized session in a non-Willow controlled test studio; 0 amendments and 0 clinical_audit_events. anon, authenticated and service_role are all NOLOGIN — only authenticator (PostgREST) and postgres can connect, and PostgREST cannot call a function it has no EXECUTE on.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: tests/db/clinical-finalization-retired.db.test.ts exists as the fresh-DB suite asserting the retirement posture. I read the inventory, not a green run. The classification rests on the applied migration text and the supplied hosted facts (revoked EXECUTE, pinned flags, NOLOGIN roles), not on a test result.
findings.missing_evidence: No two-transaction barrier test was ever written for finalizer-versus-child-write, and none should be now — the code path it would exercise is unreachable. I cannot prove from source whether the race ever occurred historically; the single legacy finalized session's snapshot hash still re-derives per the supplied hosted facts, which is consistent with (but not proof of) that one record having been signed cleanly.
findings.rationale: The race requires a finalizer transaction to run concurrently with a child write. There is no longer any way to start a finalizer transaction: the RPC's EXECUTE is revoked from every runtime role, no application code calls it, the enabling flags are pinned false by validated CHECKs so the studios-owners UPDATE policy cannot re-enable them, and even a hypothetical direct status UPDATE is refused by the 0159 §3 transition trigger while a snapshot INSERT is refused by the §4 trigger. Both prerequisites of the failure scenario ("two overlapping authenticated requests against the same draft session" where one of them finalizes) are therefore unsatisfiable. Nothing about ordinary concurrent charting is a defect here — sessions are, by explicit product decision, ordinary editable operational records with no signed artifact to be inconsistent with, so a child write committing after another transaction read the parent has no integrity consequence. The audit's recommended fix (take a per-session FOR UPDATE in every clinical mutation) is actively unsafe and must not be applied: 0159:109-117 records a REPRODUCED 40P01 deadlock against soft_delete_session_area's lock order. Severity P1 to P3, superseded rather than fixed, because the capability was withdrawn rather than the interleaving being made safe.
findings.remediation_dependency: None. Do NOT implement the recommended per-session FOR UPDATE protocol — 0159:109-117 documents a reproduced 40P01 deadlock against soft_delete_session_area's lock order; if a future feature genuinely needs encounter-level serialization it must use FOR NO KEY UPDATE.
findings.rollout_required: None. 0159 is applied and deployed; nothing further is required for this finding.
findings.acceptance_evidence: Source-stated acceptance criteria (Hone_Independent_Audit_2026-07-27.md): DB integration test with two independent transactions and barriers: child mutation pauses after authorization, finalizer completes, child commit must block then fail; repeat for each child table and structured areas.

findings.affected_roles: None reachable. anon, authenticated and service_role hold no EXECUTE on build_session_snapshot and are NOLOGIN; the owner retains it only for read-only re-derivation, and INSERT into the ledgers is refused for every role including the owner (a BEFORE INSERT row trigger, not a privilege check).
findings.exact_current_source: supabase/migrations/0159_retire_signed_clinical_records.sql:190-191 (`revoke all on function public.build_session_snapshot(uuid) from public, anon, authenticated, service_role` — the owner alone keeps it, solely for read-only re-derivation of the legacy hash); :287-317 (guard_retired_signed_ledger_insert + the three BEFORE INSERT triggers clinical_record_snapshots_retired_no_insert / clinical_record_amendments_retired_no_insert / clinical_audit_events_retired_no_insert make it impossible to write a new snapshot even if a grant were restored later); :175-183 (finalize_session, the only producer, EXECUTE-revoked); :319-324 (table comments reclassify all three ledgers as RETIRED legacy evidence only); :458-463 (truncate/references/trigger revoked from public/anon/authenticated/service_role on all three ledgers, so "fully immutable" is now literally true); :68-70 ("No snapshot v2. No structured-area signed-correction framework. Those are retired, not deferred."); :591-595 (the read-only operator query that re-derives the ONE legacy content_hash). No application code references build_session_snapshot or any snapshot table — repo-wide grep across app, lib and components returns only lib/types/database.ts:35,38.
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: Hosted facts (authoritative, supplied): EXECUTE revoked from public/anon/authenticated/service_role on all 10 retired functions including build_session_snapshot; INSERT blocked on all three signed ledgers; exactly ONE legacy finalized session and ONE snapshot exist, in a NON-Willow controlled test studio, and its hash still re-derives; 0 amendments; 0 clinical_audit_events; Willow has ZERO non-draft sessions; NO snapshot v2 and NO signed-correction framework will ever return.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: tests/db/clinical-finalization-retired.db.test.ts and tests/migrations/0159-retire-signed-clinical-records.test.ts exist; I read the inventory only, not a run. The supplied hosted fact that the ONE legacy snapshot's content_hash still re-derives to a match is the only behavioural evidence about snapshot content, and it speaks to stability of that one row, not to completeness of the schema.
findings.missing_evidence: I did not read build_session_snapshot's body at 0119 to enumerate exactly which columns it omits, because the answer cannot change the disposition — the function is unexecutable and no new snapshot can be inserted. I therefore neither confirm nor refute the audit's specific claim that session_block_areas, the 0155 probe-inventory columns and the 0156 numbing_notes column are absent from the serialized shape. If someone ever needs that answer for the single archived artifact, it must be settled by reading 0119's function body, not by a test.
findings.rationale: The finding's harm is that a verifier could call a hash valid while the snapshot fails to represent structured areas or the later 0155 probe-inventory / 0156 numbing fields. That harm requires snapshots to be a live product surface. They are not: build_session_snapshot cannot be executed by any runtime role, its only producer (finalize_session) is likewise revoked, and even a restored grant would hit a BEFORE INSERT trigger on all three ledgers. Exactly one snapshot exists in production, it belongs to a non-Willow controlled test studio, it is retained deliberately unchanged as legacy evidence, and it is frozen by the 0119 guard now that the 0120 GUC bypass is removed — so its completeness is a historical property of a single archived artifact, not a live integrity contract anyone relies on. Willow has zero non-draft sessions, so no Willow record has ever been snapshotted. The audit's fix — a versioned canonical snapshot schema covering every clinically authoritative field — is precisely what the product decision forbids, and its rollout note ("store snapshot_schema_version, preserve legacy verification") describes building the retired system. Severity P1 to P3; nothing to remediate.
findings.remediation_dependency: None. Explicitly do NOT build a versioned canonical snapshot schema, a snapshot_schema_version column, or any completeness contract — that is the retired capability.
findings.rollout_required: None. 0159 is applied and deployed. Do not rewrite, rehash or delete the single legacy snapshot; it is retained unchanged by design.
findings.acceptance_evidence: Source-stated acceptance criteria (Hone_Independent_Audit_2026-07-27.md): Golden DB tests create records differing one clinically meaningful field at a time and assert canonical snapshot/hash differences; verify round-trip rendering and export from the snapshot.

findings.current_title: Intake-to-client profile sync has no version predicate — but it is fill-only-if-null and append-only, so the stated overwrite scenario is not reproducible; a narrow read-then-write lost-update window remains
findings.affected_roles: service_role only (the sync runs through createAdminClient() on the server; the client submitting the intake is unauthenticated and token-scoped). No browser role can invoke the sync directly. The practitioner side of the race is an ordinary authenticated studio member using the client edit form.
findings.exact_current_source: app/intake/[token]/actions.ts:186-208 (the submit CAS: `.update({... status:'submitted' ...}).eq('id', v.intake_id).eq('status','in_progress')` with a zero-rows race-loser branch — this part is sound); :215 (`await syncIntakeToClient(merged, existing.client_id)` runs only in the CAS winner branch, outside any transaction spanning the two tables); :254-269 (the documented field-authority contract: emergency_contact_name/_phone, date_of_birth, pronouns, address are FILL-ONLY-IF-NULL; allergies is APPEND-ONLY, never overwritten, never deleted); :293-309 (admin client reads the six current client values); :311-341 (patch construction — every scalar field is gated on `&& !client.<field>`, so a practitioner-entered value present at read time is preserved; allergies concatenates existing + a dated "From client intake" marker); :342 (`if (Object.keys(patch).length === 0) return;`); :344-347 (`await admin.from('clients').update(patch).eq('id', clientId)` — NO version, updated_at or is-null predicate, and no row-count check); :348-350 (failures are logged and swallowed by design — the intake submit is the source of truth and is not rolled back). Critically, `phone` and `email` are NOT in the synced field set at all (:296-297 select list and :311-341 patch), so the audit's headline example of a practitioner correcting the phone cannot be clobbered by this path.
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: The supplied hosted facts cover the clinical-retirement objects (0159), the lineage triggers (0160), the 86-table ACL survey, NOLOGIN role reality and the 139 SECURITY DEFINER functions. They say nothing about public.client_intake_forms or public.clients contents, about whether any intake submission has ever overlapped a practitioner profile edit, or about row counts on those tables. The one indirectly relevant fact is that this path runs through createAdminClient() (service_role, server-only) rather than through a browser role, so no RLS or grant fact bears on it.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: None found. tests/app/intake/ contains only intake-submit-notification.test.ts; no test exercises syncIntakeToClient, the field-authority rules, or concurrent profile writes. The submit-side CAS (`.eq('status','in_progress')` with a zero-rows loser branch) is the only concurrency control on this path and it protects the intake row only, exactly as the audit's test-limitations note said.
findings.missing_evidence: I could not prove whether this interleaving has ever actually occurred in production — that would need a query correlating client_intake_forms.submitted_at against clients row-modification history, and no such history table is guaranteed to exist for public.clients; I did not query production. There is no test at all for syncIntakeToClient (tests/app/intake/ contains only intake-submit-notification.test.ts), so there is no two-connection barrier test proving or disproving the window, and no unit test pinning the fill-only-if-null / append-only contract against regression. I also did not audit the reverse direction in depth — a practitioner's full-record client edit form has a much wider read-to-write window (page load to submit) and could equally clobber freshly synced intake values; that reverse race is a separate, unfiled concern I am flagging rather than classifying.
findings.rationale: I read the actual sync and the audit's central premise does not hold. There IS a field-level merge contract, written down and enforced at app/intake/[token]/actions.ts:254-341: five scalar fields are fill-only-if-null and allergies is append-only. A practitioner value that exists when the sync reads the row is preserved, not overwritten — and phone/email, the audit's own example fields, are never synced at all. What remains is a genuine but much narrower defect: the read at :293-309 and the write at :344-347 are two separate service-role statements with no predicate tying them together, so in the window between them (one round trip, tens of milliseconds, and only in the CAS-winner branch of a submit) a practitioner write can be lost. Two concrete residuals: (a) a field that was NULL at read time and is set to X by a practitioner mid-window is overwritten with the intake value; (b) allergies — the clinically loaded one — is written as `stale_existing + intake_text`, so a concurrent practitioner allergy edit inside that window is discarded, defeating the append-only intent. Both are real, both are trivially fixable with `.is('<field>', null)` predicates and a re-read-and-append for allergies, and neither matches the P1 scenario as filed. I keep the status OPEN rather than FALSE_POSITIVE because the lost-update window is real and does touch an allergy field; I drop the severity to P3 because the window is one round trip wide, requires exact-instant concurrency between a client's final submit click and a practitioner's profile save, is bounded to fields that were empty (or to an append), and cannot silently delete anything.
findings.remediation_dependency: None blocking. The minimal fix is self-contained in app/intake/[token]/actions.ts:344-347: add `.is('<field>', null)` predicates for the five fill-only-if-null columns so the write asserts the same emptiness the read observed, and re-read-then-append allergies (or move the append into a small SECURITY DEFINER command that reads and writes in one statement). A visible "profile differs from submitted intake" reconciliation surface, as the audit suggested, is a product decision and not required to close the lost-update window.
findings.rollout_required: Code-only; ships with an ordinary Vercel deploy. Do NOT retroactively re-run historical intake syncs — the append-only allergy text is already in the clients rows and a replay would duplicate it.
findings.acceptance_evidence: Source-stated acceptance criteria (Hone_Independent_Audit_2026-07-27.md): Two-connection DB test: update client after intake read but before sync; command must preserve the newer value or return a conflict requiring review.

findings.current_title: "Mark reviewed" accepts an unsubmitted (in_progress) intake and any intake in the studio — one UI click creates a false clinical-review signal and permanently locks the client out of finishing their intake
findings.affected_roles: authenticated (any active practitioner who is a member of the studio — the action runs through the user-scoped createClient() at :40, so the 0087 studio-membership UPDATE policy is the only authorization; no owner role is needed). Cross-studio is correctly blocked by `.eq('studio_id', studio.id)` plus RLS. Inactive practitioners are rejected at :36-38.
findings.exact_current_source: app/(app)/clients/[id]/intake/actions.ts:41-52 — `supabase.from('client_intake_forms').update({ status:'reviewed', reviewed_at, reviewed_by, practitioner_notes }).eq('id', intakeId).eq('studio_id', studio.id).is('deleted_at', null)`: no `.eq('status','submitted')` predicate, no `.eq('client_id', clientId)` predicate (clientId is accepted at :26-28 and used only for revalidatePath at :54-55), no `.select()` and therefore no affected-row check — a zero-row update returns `{ ok: true }`. app/(app)/clients/[id]/intake/page.tsx:336-341 renders `<IntakeReviewForm ... alreadyReviewed={intake.status === 'reviewed'} />` UNCONDITIONALLY, including when the branch at :281-286 has just printed "The client has not submitted their intake yet". app/(app)/clients/[id]/intake/IntakeReviewForm.tsx:76-85 shows the "Mark reviewed" button whenever `!alreadyReviewed` — i.e. it is on screen for an in_progress intake. supabase/migrations/0118_intake_terminal_immutability.sql:50 gates the entire guard body on `if old.status in ('submitted','reviewed')`, so an in_progress row passes through the trigger untouched and the in_progress -> reviewed transition is unguarded at the DB boundary. Consequences I traced: app/intake/[token]/actions.ts:85-87 (client's saveIntakeStepAction refuses once status is 'reviewed') and :154-156 (submitIntakeAction early-returns ok:true without ever setting submitted_at or running syncIntakeToClient), plus app/intake/[token]/page.tsx:74 (the public page treats 'reviewed' as submitted) — the client's link is silently dead. lib/intake/queries.ts:47-63 (`.in('status', ['submitted','reviewed'])`) then treats the never-submitted row as the client's intake of record. lib/dashboard/daily-prep-brief.ts:140 (`if (upcoming && input.intake !== 'reviewed') return 2`), app/(app)/dashboard/page.tsx:791 and app/(app)/calendar/[id]/page.tsx:977 all suppress their intake prompts once status is 'reviewed'. Contrast with the correctly-written sibling actions in the same file: getIntakeLinkAction:270-285 and resendIntakeEmailAction:338-353 both re-fetch the intake filtered by `.eq('studio_id')` AND `.eq('client_id')` and both explicitly reject a wrong status.
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: The supplied hosted facts are silent on client_intake_forms: they cover the 0159/0160 clinical retirement objects, the 86-table TRUNCATE/DML ACL survey of clinical tables, NOLOGIN role reality and the SECURITY DEFINER inventory. No count of in_progress-marked-reviewed rows in production was supplied, and I did not query production. The relevant hosted fact is negative: nothing in the retirement or the lineage triggers touches this table or this transition, so 0159 and 0160 neither fix nor affect it. The general fact that `authenticated` retains broad row DML is consistent with the 0087 studio-membership UPDATE policy still being what authorizes this write.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: None. A repo-wide grep for markIntakeReviewedAction across tests/ returns no file; tests/app/intake/ contains only intake-submit-notification.test.ts, and no db test in tests/db/ covers client_intake_forms transitions. So there is no draft-to-reviewed rejection test, no wrong-client test, no affected-row-count test, and no test pinning that the "Mark reviewed" button is hidden for an unsubmitted intake. This is an untested transition on a live clinical-signal field.
findings.missing_evidence: I did not query production, so I cannot say whether any live intake row is currently in status='reviewed' with submitted_at IS NULL — that single read-only query (`select count(*) from public.client_intake_forms where status='reviewed' and submitted_at is null and deleted_at is null`, grouped by studio) is the decisive evidence for whether this has already fired at Willow and should be run before choosing between a plain guard and a guard-plus-reconciliation-report. I also did not verify by execution that the 0118 trigger permits the in_progress -> reviewed update; that conclusion is read off the `if old.status in ('submitted','reviewed')` gate at line 50 with no other branch covering an in_progress OLD row.
findings.rationale: This one is real, unmitigated, and reachable through the ordinary deployed UI — not merely through a crafted request. The review page renders the answers-so-far of an unsubmitted intake along with an amber "the client has not submitted yet" notice, and directly beneath it renders a live "Mark reviewed" button; one click writes status='reviewed', reviewed_at and reviewed_by. Migration 0118 does not catch it because its whole body is conditioned on the OLD status already being terminal, so the in_progress -> reviewed edge is the one transition nobody guards. The consequences are worse than the audit stated. First, a false clinical signal: lib/intake/queries.ts selects `in ('submitted','reviewed')` as the latest intake of record, so partial answers — including partially-completed allergy and EpiPen questions — become the client's intake of record, and the daily-prep brief, dashboard and calendar-day views all stop flagging that an intake is outstanding. Second, and unfiled by the audit, the client is bricked: their tokenized link now refuses every save and the submit path early-returns ok:true, so submitted_at is never set and syncIntakeToClient never runs; the practitioner must issue an entirely new intake to recover, and the answers can never be completed. Separately, the missing client_id predicate means a same-studio intake belonging to a different client can be marked reviewed (the page-level deep-link resolver at page.tsx:130-141 does check `looked.client_id === id`, so this half needs a crafted server-action POST, and the two sibling actions in the same file show the intended pattern was simply omitted here). findings.rationale: This is a live authorization-boundary defect, not a missing feature, and it is reachable today by a real browser user. A logged-in studio member holds the anon key and their own JWT, and appointments carries a single FOR ALL membership policy with the Supabase default ALL grant to authenticated. A raw PostgREST POST/PATCH/DELETE therefore reaches the table directly and skips, in one request, every control the 0142→0152 command series was built to impose: the practitioner_capacity_booking_enabled kill switch, the owner-only gate on retargeting another practitioner, the owner-only duration override, the authoritative duration derived from a locked service row, the future-time check, validate_appointment_availability, and the mandatory appointment_audit row. Three consequences make this materially worse than a policy-only bypass. First, the one guard that does fire for every writer — the 0152 soft-buffer trigger — is disarmed by a column the writer controls: setting booked_outside_availability=true in the same PATCH turns the buffer off, converting an owner-only privilege into a self-service one. Second, appointment_audit is ON DELETE CASCADE from appointments, so an authenticated member does not merely bypass the audit trail, they can erase it by deleting the appointment row. Third, status is money-adjacent: forging status='completed' satisfies the session-payment eligibility gate before the appointment has ended, and live payments are on at Willow. What still holds is real and should not be overstated: the per-resource GiST exclusion on studio_calendar_reservations (0134/0152) is never bypassable, so a true double-book still fails with 23P01; 0151's composite same-studio FKs stop cross-studio client/service/practitioner references; RLS still blocks cross-studio rows entirely; and 0090's hashing trigger still fires. So this is intra-tenant privilege separation and audit integrity, not tenant isolation. It stays P1 because it is an active, browser-reachable authorization defect with an audit-destruction and a payment-gate consequence, and because the fix is unusually cheap: I traced every appointment write in the deployed tree and all of them go through the service-role admin client (app/book/[slug]/actions.ts:770-790, app/(app)/calendar/actions.ts:1114-1250, app/(app)/calendar/postcare-auto-send.ts:150-205, app/(app)/calendar/move-appointment-actions.ts:352, app/cancel/[token]/actions.ts, app/reschedule/[token]/actions.ts, app/manage/[token]/actions.ts, app/api/cron/appointment-reminders/route.ts), and the browser Supabase client is used only for login (the sole importer of lib/supabase/client.ts is app/(auth)/login/page.tsx). Revoking authenticated INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on appointments is therefore invisible to the application — unlike the clinical tables of L18, this needs no 26-call-site migration first. I did not lower the severity because Willow is one studio: the guidance is explicit that an active authorization defect is not discounted for tenant count, and non-owner practitioners can exist independently of the (currently OFF) capacity flags.
findings.remediation_dependency: Independent of L18 and of the clinical work. Two coupled steps: (1) revoke insert, update, delete on public.appointments from anon, authenticated (SELECT retained — the user-scoped server client reads appointments in lib/booking/queries.ts, app/(app)/calendar/[id]/page.tsx:96, app/(app)/dashboard/page.tsx:126 and lib/supabase/queries.ts); no app change is needed because every write already uses the service-role admin client. (2) Close the self-granted override: make booked_outside_availability writable only by the owner-gated commands (a BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE trigger that refuses a true value not stamped by create_internal_appointment_v2 / move_or_reassign_appointment), otherwise a service-role-mediated path could still be tricked into carrying it. Optionally add narrow cancel/complete/no-show wrappers, but those RPCs already exist (practitioner_cancel_appointment, mark_appointment_complete, mark_appointment_no_show) and are already service_role-only.

findings.rationale: Downgraded from P1 to P2 after tracing what the DB actually enforces on the public path. The audit's core worry — an unserialized check-then-insert — is only half true. Every appointment INSERT, including this direct public one, fires appointments_sync_calendar_reservation_trg, which mirrors into studio_calendar_reservations, where a single GiST exclusion covers appointments, timed blocks, full-day blockouts AND recurring-break occurrences; plus the two hard actual-overlap GiST exclusions on appointments itself; plus enforce_appointment_buffer (HB001), which 0152 was written specifically so the public direct insert cannot lose buffer enforcement. Postgres exclusion constraints serialize concurrent inserters, so the races the finding names for overrides/blockouts/breaks/buffer/double-book are closed at the DB and surface to the booker as the safe "no longer available" copy (actions.ts:800-815). What is genuinely NOT serialized and NOT DB-enforced on this path: the working-hours window (studio_availability_default/_overrides are not mirrored into reservations), services.active flipping to false between the recheck and the insert, and the capacity pause flag (F-SCHED-002). Those races commit an appointment slightly outside newly-narrowed hours or on a just-archived service — visible on the calendar, recoverable, not an integrity or authorization breach, and the window is the sub-second gap between recheck and insert. The one defect here that needs no race at all and IS deterministically reachable today: a new public booker's clients row is inserted before the appointment insert, so ANY appointment-insert failure (23P01, HB001, or any other error) returns an error to the visitor while leaving a brand-new client record in the studio, with no compensating delete. findings.exact_hosted_evidence: Not applicable — this is pure application code with no DB or flag dependency. It is in the deployed bundle at production SHA c64366c9.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: No test executed. I read the pinning unit tests directly; they encode the current (incorrect) mapping as expected, which is exactly the false-confidence pattern the audit flagged.

findings.rationale: Technically confirmed exactly as written, including the audit's test-limitation claim: tests/lib/booking/tz-dst-two-pass.test.ts:127-139 deliberately PINS the wrong-by-an-hour mapping as expected behaviour, so the suite provides false confidence rather than rejecting the gap. No caller performs the round-trip check (render the computed instant back to a local HH:MM and compare to what was typed) that would catch it, and no caller offers an occurrence choice for the repeated hour. Severity drops from P1 to P3 on reachability and blast radius, not on correctness. To hit the gap a practitioner must enter a wall time inside a one-hour window that occurs twice a year at 02:00-03:00 local (spring) or 01:00-02:00 local (fall); every reachable entry point is an owner-gated custom-time surface (move dialog custom time, quick-book override, client-page override, typed calendar blocks) or generated slots, and generated slots only reach the gap if a studio's open window covers 02:00 — a beauty/electrolysis studio's published hours do not. The consequence is also narrower than the finding states: once written, the row is a UTC instant, so reminders, calendar rendering and Google events all agree with each other — they agree on the SHIFTED time. So this is a silent one-hour mis-write against practitioner intent (spring) and an unreachable second occurrence (fall), not a cross-system inconsistency. Whole-local-day intervals are separately correct and tested (lib/booking/tz.ts:156-166 isAllDayInterval; tests/lib/booking/all-day-block-dst.test.ts), and the 23h/25h day arithmetic is right.

findings.rollout_required: App-only deploy. findings.current_title: Sentry receives raw bearer credentials embedded in URL path segments (intake, portal, appointment-manage and calendar-feed tokens)
findings.affected_roles: Anonymous/unauthenticated visitors are the primary exposure — every one of these six routes is reachable without a Supabase session, which is the whole point of a bearer token in the path. Practitioners are exposed via the calendar-feed token. The party who can exploit a leaked credential is anyone with access to the Sentry project or to data disclosed by that processor; no Hone role or database grant is involved.
findings.exact_current_source: lib/observability/sentry-scrub.ts:183-199 scrubRequest — deletes cookies, headers and query_string, but line 189 does request.url = redactString(request.url.split("?")[0]), i.e. the PATH is deliberately preserved and only value-pattern scrubbed. lib/observability/sentry-scrub.ts:91-98 the value patterns: JWT_RE = /\beyJ[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+\.[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+\.[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+/g requires THREE dot-separated segments; BEARER_RE requires a literal 'Bearer ' prefix; SUPABASE_TOKEN_RE matches only sb-*-auth-token / sbp_ / service_role. lib/observability/sentry-scrub.ts:235-291 scrubEventCommon never touches event.transaction (the transaction NAME is not scrubbed at all). Token routes that put a credential in the path: app/intake/[token], app/manage/[token], app/cancel/[token], app/reschedule/[token], app/portal/verify/[token], app/calendar-feed/[token]. Token formats that DEFEAT the regexes: lib/intake/tokens.ts:4-5 and :64-72 — format is base64url(payload).base64url(signature), i.e. TWO segments beginning 'eyJ' (base64 of '{"intake_id"...'), so JWT_RE's mandatory third segment never matches and the token passes through verbatim; lib/booking/tokens.ts:63 returns the identical two-segment `${payloadB64}.${sig}`; lib/calendar-feed/token.ts:34-35 generateCalendarFeedToken returns randomBytes(32).toString("base64url") — an opaque dot-free random string that matches none of the five patterns. Sentry is initialized and enabled with a hardcoded DSN in all three runtimes: sentry.server.config.ts:16-26, sentry.edge.config.ts, instrumentation-client.ts:25-35, and wired at build time by next.config.ts:1 withSentryConfig with tunnelRoute "/monitoring" (:127). lib/observability/sentry-scrub.ts:323-325 tracesSampleRate() returns 0.1 in production, so ~10% of pageloads/requests on these routes emit a transaction carrying request.url. Token lifetime: lib/intake/tokens.ts:25-27 states intake tokens live ~weeks; lib/calendar-feed/token.ts has no expiry concept at all.
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: Sentry is live in production — it was merged and deployed at ed23a7a with no env kill switch in the config (the DSN is a hardcoded literal, not an env-conditional), so every production deployment initializes it. Migrations 0159 and 0160 are clinical-lineage work and touch nothing in the observability path; git log shows no commit touching lib/observability/sentry-scrub.ts after the original hardening, so the exact-head file is the deployed file. The NOLOGIN/PostgREST reachability facts do not mitigate this at all — the leak path is HTTPS egress from the Next.js process to a third-party SaaS, not a database grant.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: None, and the gap is verifiable: tests/lib/observability/sentry-scrub.test.ts contains no occurrence of 'intake', '/manage/', 'path' or 'transaction'. Every existing assertion covers key-based redaction and the five value patterns. This is exactly the audit's stated test limitation — the suite passes while the defect is present, which is why a source-string or green-suite argument must not be accepted as evidence of a fix here.
findings.missing_evidence: I cannot prove from source whether any such event has ALREADY been transmitted to Sentry — that requires querying the Sentry project's stored events (search by route pattern, never exporting raw URLs). I also cannot confirm from the repository whether Sentry's data region is US or EU, or the project's retention window and member list, all of which bound the actual blast radius. Sentry error events are unsampled, so the volume depends entirely on how often these routes error in production, which is not knowable from the tree.
findings.rationale: CONFIRMED precisely, and the audit's mechanism holds up under direct inspection with one detail it did not have: I can show exactly WHY the regexes miss. Hone's intake and appointment tokens are two-segment HMAC tokens whose payload base64 begins 'eyJ', which looks like a JWT but has only one dot — JWT_RE demands two dots, so the token is emitted verbatim. The calendar-feed token is a dot-free 32-byte base64url random string matching none of the five value patterns. scrubRequest explicitly keeps the path (line 189 splits on '?' and keeps the left side), and event.transaction is never scrubbed anywhere in the file. So an exception, a fetch/xhr breadcrumb, or one of the 10% sampled production transactions on any of six route families ships a replayable bearer credential to a US third-party processor. I keep this at P1 rather than raising or lowering it: raising to P0 is not warranted because exploitation requires access to the Sentry project (or a breach at that processor) rather than being directly attacker-triggerable, and the intake/appointment tokens expire; lowering is not warranted because the credentials in question unlock client intake health answers, appointment cancellation/reschedule control, portal verification and a practitioner's entire private availability feed (the calendar-feed token never expires and per F-CAL-001 has no rotate/revoke UI), the leak is continuous rather than hypothetical at 10% trace sampling, and no compensating control exists anywhere on this path. PostHog's strong route boundary (instrumentation-client.ts:39-83, which drops every browser event on token routes) does not extend to Sentry — the two SDKs are initialized side by side in the same file, which makes the asymmetry unusually easy to miss and unusually easy to fix.
findings.remediation_dependency: None — fully self-contained and code-only, confined to lib/observability/sentry-scrub.ts. Three changes: (1) in scrubRequest, canonicalize the path against the known bearer-route prefixes (/intake/, /manage/, /cancel/, /reschedule/, /portal/verify/, /calendar-feed/) to a template such as /intake/[token] before assigning request.url; (2) apply the same canonicalization to event.transaction, which is currently never scrubbed; (3) apply it to the breadcrumb URL path at :217-222, which today only strips the query string. Add a generic opaque-high-entropy-segment fallback so a future token route is safe by default. Operationally, treat any credential already sent as potentially disclosed: intake tokens expire on their own within weeks, but the calendar-feed token does not and should be rotated — which itself depends on F-CAL-001's missing rotate/revoke capability.
findings.depends_on_by_pr_note: PR-05 (the go-forward Sentry scrub) depends on nothing. The DURABLE half — invalidating tokens already transmitted — depends on F-CAL-001's missing rotate/revoke capability, which is not scheduled in this tranche. The containment fix must not wait for it.
findings.rollout_required: Standard Vercel production deploy of the app; no migration, no flag, no data operation. Deploy the scrub fix BEFORE any widening of tracesSampleRate. After deploying, review Sentry retention and access, and search historical events by route PATTERN only — do not export raw event URLs, since that would move the leaked tokens into a second location.
findings.Willow_risk: Live at Willow today. Replayable intake, portal and calendar-feed bearer tokens are transmitted to Sentry on every captured event, so a third-party service holds credentials that grant access to a real client's clinical surfaces. Code-only to fix.
findings.acceptance_evidence: Source-stated acceptance criteria (Hone_Independent_Audit_2026-07-27.md): Sentry scrub tests with realistic opaque tokens in request URL, transaction, span description, breadcrumb and exception context; assert the token never appears in serialized event JSON.

Table and access model: supabase/migrations/0010_booking_v1.sql:217-225 defines appointment_audit with details jsonb and appointment_id ... references public.appointments(id) ON DELETE CASCADE not null; :242 enables RLS; :279-289 policy appointment_audit_member_read grants SELECT to studio members of the owning appointment; :290-299 appointment_audit_member_insert. Deletion chain: appointments.client_id at 0010:178 is references public.clients(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, so client -> appointments -> appointment_audit cascades coherently. findings.exact_hosted_evidence: No hosted schema change is involved; the write is application-level into a table that has existed since migration 0010, and migration max 0160 contains nothing touching appointment_audit. git log shows app/book/[slug]/actions.ts was last modified by c0254ac (the 0152 manual-override booking work), so the exact-head line 880 is the deployed behaviour. Willow's live public-booking volume and therefore the number of affected audit rows is not established by the hosted facts supplied.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: Not executed, and no minimization test exists. The audit's observation that 'audit-event existence tests often reward richer payloads without checking minimization' is borne out: no test asserts that raw email, phone or free-text notes are absent from any audit or ops payload. Confirmation here is static — the literal object at line 880 plus the policy definitions in 0010.
findings.missing_evidence: I cannot determine from source how many public-booking audit rows exist in production or how many carry non-empty notes, so the size of the historical remediation is unknown. I also could not find any code that redacts appointments.notes on request, so the redaction-divergence scenario is currently hypothetical rather than an established workflow — if no note-redaction capability exists at all, the residual risk is smaller still and this could reasonably be recorded as an accepted limitation with disclosure.
findings.rationale: The mechanism is CONFIRMED verbatim — line 880 really does write raw email and raw free-text notes into audit JSON that duplicate the canonical appointment and client records. But three properties of the current source materially reduce the impact the audit assigned, and I verified each rather than assuming: (1) the audience is identical, not expanded — appointment_audit_member_read scopes SELECT to studio members of the owning appointment, exactly the same people who can already read appointments.notes and clients.email, so no new party gains access; (2) deletion is coherent, not divergent — the FK is ON DELETE CASCADE up through appointments and clients, so deleting the client or the appointment removes the audit copy automatically, which was the audit's main stated harm ('deletion/export policies may differ') and it does not hold for deletion; (3) anon has no read path to this table. What genuinely remains is narrower: a REDACTION divergence rather than a deletion divergence — if a practitioner edits or clears sensitive text from appointments.notes in response to a client request, the original text survives in the audit JSON with nothing pointing at it — plus the fact that the studio export does not include appointment_audit, so this copy is invisible to a data-access request. That is a real data-minimization defect but a low-severity one, so P2 -> P3. It is not fixed and should not be closed.
findings.remediation_dependency: None blocking for the go-forward fix, which is a one-line change at app/book/[slug]/actions.ts:880 to store minimized metadata (source, plus booleans or lengths such as has_notes / notes_length, plus the already-present client_id and appointment_id via the appointment) instead of the raw values. Redacting the HISTORICAL payloads is a separate, dependent decision: it must not happen before a retention policy exists (this overlaps F-RET-001), and it should be coordinated with the export-completeness work (F-DATA-001) so that whatever the audit table retains is either exported or provably out of scope.
findings.rollout_required: App deploy only for the go-forward minimization; no migration, no flag. Historical redaction, if approved, would be a one-off authorized data operation (an UPDATE stripping details->>'email' and details->>'notes' on rows where details->>'source' = 'public_booking'), which must be run under the normal prod-authorization process and only after a retention decision is recorded.
findings.acceptance_evidence: Source-stated acceptance criteria (Hone_Independent_Audit_2026-07-27.md): Tests assert raw email, phone and arbitrary notes never appear in audit/log/ops payloads.

findings.current_title: Treatment-image upload can orphan private storage objects with no reconciler, and archive never deletes bytes at all
findings.affected_roles: practitioner and owner (uploaders/archivers); clients whose photo bytes persist after deletion
findings.exact_current_source: app/(app)/clients/[id]/images/actions.ts:173-196 — service-role upload of sanitized bytes to the private bucket happens FIRST (admin.storage.from(TREATMENT_IMAGES_BUCKET).upload(storagePath, ..., {upsert:false})). :199-211 — the RLS-client metadata insert into treatment_images happens SECOND. :212-235 — on insert failure it attempts admin.storage.remove([storagePath]) and, if that also fails, records a severity:"critical" ops alert with event "treatment_image_orphan_cleanup_failed"; then returns a generic error. There is no durable intent record written before the upload, no retry of the removal, and no reconciler: a repo-wide grep for "orphan" outside tests hits only this file, block-actions.ts, google-calendar-actions.ts and admin/studios/new/actions.ts — none of them scan the images bucket. vercel.json registers 3 crons, none of which touch storage. Additionally :351-387 archiveTreatmentImageAction only stamps deleted_at/deleted_by — the storage object is never removed on archive, so archived photos are a second, guaranteed class of untracked-forever bytes. lib/ops/alerts.ts recordOpsAlert is the only signal and it is best-effort (see F-OPS-005).
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: Not re-queried today. No hosted fact covers treatment_images row count, ops_alerts rows with event='treatment_image_orphan_cleanup_failed', or the object count in the private bucket, so no production orphan has been demonstrated or ruled out.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: tests/app/clients/treatment-image-hardening.test.ts, treatment-image-content-validation.test.ts and treatment-photo-attach-context.test.ts exist; the cleanup path is exercised with mocks only, which by construction cannot prove eventual reconciliation.

findings.rationale: Confirmed exactly. Upload-then-insert with best-effort compensating delete and no durable ledger or reconciler is precisely what the code does. The engineering around it is otherwise strong (private bucket, no public URLs, server-generated path, EXIF-stripping re-encode, path validated before signing), so the residual risk is narrow: it needs a metadata insert failure AND a storage delete failure in the same request. The orphan is not a confidentiality problem — the bucket is private, no public URL exists, and getTreatmentImageSignedUrlAction (:244-305) only signs paths read off a verified treatment_images row, so an orphan can never be served. The harm is retention and cost: bytes that no export, no deletion request and no purge can ever reach because nothing knows they exist. I am also counting the archive path as part of this finding rather than a separate one, because it produces the same untracked-bytes end state deterministically on every photo deletion. P2 is right — not reachable as an access defect, but a real cross-system consistency gap that compounds F-RET-001.
findings.remediation_dependency: Should be built together with F-RET-001, because a bucket-vs-metadata reconciler and a retention purge job are the same walk over the same two inventories. Minimal fix needs no migration: a scheduled route that lists bucket objects under each studio prefix, left-joins treatment_images by storage_path, and quarantines/alerts on unmatched objects older than a safety window — plus removing bytes (or scheduling their removal) when archiveTreatmentImageAction soft-deletes. findings.rollout_required: Reconciler ships as a new authenticated cron route registered in vercel.json with CRON_SECRET, in report-only mode first (alert, never delete) until it has run clean against production for a full cycle. findings.affected_roles: owner (sole invoker); the serverless function's shared capacity
findings.exact_current_source: app/(app)/settings/data/actions.ts:47-198 issues 16 unbounded reads via Promise.all — no .limit(), no .range(), no pagination on any of them (clients, sessions, electrolysis_entries, laser_entries, appointments, treatment_plans, treatment_plan_stages, session_blocks, the four record_keeping tables including record_keeping_audit_events which is append-only and grows without bound). :334-339 adds a 17th unbounded read of session_block_areas. Client side app/(app)/settings/data/ExportButton.tsx:6-13 atob()s the whole string into a third full copy in the browser before creating the Blob. Peak server residency ≈ all rows + all CSV strings + zip internals + uint8array + base64 string, concurrently. No streaming, no object storage, no job queue, no size cap, no timeout guard, no cancellation.
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: Hosted facts do not include Willow row counts. Known scale signals from the hosted record are all small: 6 live charges, 1 GCal event, 0 copy-ledger rows, 0 non-draft sessions at Willow. There is no hosted evidence of a large studio, and no evidence of an export OOM/timeout.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: None. tests/app/settings/data/export-owner-gate.test.ts is a source-string test. No fixture exercises large row counts, memory or timeout behaviour.
findings.missing_evidence: No load test and no measured memory profile at any scale; the actual row counts at Willow and the serverless memory limit configured for the deployment were not established, so the failure threshold is unquantified.
findings.rationale: Confirmed exactly as written. Every read is unbounded, the archive is fully materialized, and the base64 duplication through the server-action boundary is real and adds a second full copy on the server plus a third in the browser. Two nuances the audit did not state: the export also holds several derived arrays and lookup Maps alongside the raw rows, so peak memory is meaningfully higher than 'rows + zip'; and record_keeping_audit_events is monotonically growing and unbounded, which makes memory scale with studio age rather than just client count. Against that, the code path runs today without failing because production volume is tiny, and the failure mode is a clean error (OOM/timeout), not corruption or disclosure. production_reachable is true in the strict sense that a real owner triggers this exact code in one click today; the adverse outcome requires data volume Willow does not have. findings.current_title: Anonymous "next available" performs an unbounded sequential day-by-day scan, up to ~370 days x 4 DB round-trips per single public request

findings.exact_current_source: app/book/[slug]/actions.ts:245-330 fetchNextAvailableDateAction. :309 `while (cursor <= horizon.maxDateStr && scans < MAX_NEXT_AVAILABLE_SCAN_DAYS)` with :311 `await getAvailableSlots(...)` inside the loop and :327 cursor advanced one day at a time — fully sequential, no batching, no early materialized-availability query. :243 MAX_NEXT_AVAILABLE_SCAN_DAYS = maxPublicBookingHorizonDays() + 14 = 386 (lib/booking/horizon.ts:41-45, 12 months x 31 days). Effective bound is the studio's own horizon: lib/booking/horizon.ts:22 default 3 months, :28 DAYS_PER_HORIZON_MONTH = 31, so 93 days by default and up to 372 if a studio picks 12 months. Per iteration, lib/booking/slots.ts:147-249 issues up to 4 sequential reads with capacity OFF — studio_blockouts (:147-152, short-circuits the day if hit), then getStudioWideOverrideDaySafe (:222) then getStudioWideDaySafe (:226), then studio_calendar_reservations (:245-250). So an empty-calendar studio costs ~370 sequential round-trips per anonymous request at default horizon, ~1,480 at 12 months. Caller is anonymous: app/book/[slug]/PublicBookForm.tsx:313 invokes it from the public page. The only guard is :252-258 limitPublicSlots, which is lib/rate-limit/public.ts:204-221 — 60 requests per 60s per (hashed IP, slug), and it FAILS OPEN on limiter error or missing Upstash env (:209 returns allowed when env unset, :217-220 returns allowed on backend error). findings.rationale: Confirmed as written, with the bound made precise. The code does contain two mitigations the audit did not credit: a hard scan cap (MAX_NEXT_AVAILABLE_SCAN_DAYS) and a rate limiter. Neither closes it. The cap is derived from the maximum configurable horizon specifically so it never truncates, so it is not a work budget — it is a safety net set above the worst case. And the limiter is a documented fail-open cost dampener (lib/rate-limit/public.ts:11-15 states explicitly it is 'not an authorization control'), so during an Upstash outage or an env misconfiguration the amplification is unbounded. findings.remediation_dependency: Independent of the other findings in this batch, but should be sequenced behind the public-booking correctness/atomicity work (F-PUBLIC-001, F-SCHED-002/003) so availability is not optimized before it is correct — the audit's own rollout note. findings.rationale: Confirmed exactly as written, at the exact lines the audit implied. The ciphertext format is versioned (v1:<keyVersion>:iv:tag:ct) and AES-256-GCM fail-closed - good - but keyForVersion resolves ONLY the currently configured version; anything else returns null and both encrypt and decrypt then return encryption_key_unavailable. I drop this from P2 to P3 rather than confirming P2 because the trigger is an operator env-var change (there is no in-app rotation surface at all), the whole Google subsystem is dormant, and the realistic blast radius today is one non-Willow connection. It is a genuine unfixed design gap that must be closed before Google sync is offered to multiple studios, not a defect a user can trigger.
findings.remediation_dependency: Add a previous-key slot (GOOGLE_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS + _VERSION) inside keyForVersion, or move to KMS envelope encryption; then a bounded rewrap job that re-encrypts every stored refresh secret under the new version, plus a verification query asserting zero rows remain at the old encryption_key_version before the old key is retired. findings.unscheduled_reason: Google Calendar is dormant in production; no GCal PR is in this tranche.
findings.rollout_required: Code + Vercel env-var change (new previous-key slot), then an authorized one-off rewrap run, then old-key retirement only after a zero-remaining-rows check. Must be designed and exercised BEFORE any real key rotation, not during one.

findings.current_title: Public booking is non-transactional: a client INSERT (and an existing-client SMS-consent UPDATE) commit before the appointment INSERT, so a failed booking can leave an orphan client
findings.affected_roles: Public/unauthenticated bookers; the studio owner (Chloe) sees the polluted directory. No cross-studio exposure - every write is scoped to studio.id resolved from the slug.
findings.exact_current_source: app/book/[slug]/actions.ts:336 (publicBookAppointmentAction, unauthenticated public server action), :413-425 (rate limit before any DB work), :455-464 (public-readiness soft gate), :488-509 (slot re-verification via getAvailableSlots - returns "That time is no longer available" BEFORE any write; the `free` check is at :504), :534-540 (existing-client lookup on normalized_email, archived excluded), :615-645 (existing-client sms_consent_at / sms_consent_source UPDATE - a COMMITTED write before the appointment insert; the update begins at :624 and sets sms_consent_at at :628), :646-687 (new-client INSERT into clients at :669-672 - the second COMMITTED write before the appointment insert), :770-792 (appointment INSERT), :793-826 (failure handling: sqlstate 23P01 exclusion violation and HB001 buffer trigger both return "That time is no longer available", every other sqlstate returns the generic error - in ALL branches the client row created at :669 is already committed and is never cleaned up), :845-861 (marketing-consent insert) and :875-880 (appointment_audit insert), which correctly occur only AFTER a successful appointment insert; lib/rate-limit:228-259 (limitPublicBooking; fails OPEN on limiter outage at :255-258)
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: None queried. I have no production count of client rows with zero appointments, so I cannot say whether any orphan has actually been created at Willow.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: Not executed. I traced the full write ordering through the action line by line, including all three failure branches after the appointments insert, and confirmed no compensating delete exists anywhere in the file.
findings.missing_evidence: I did not measure how often 23P01/HB001 actually fires in production (a booking_slot_collision log event is emitted at :800-810, so the frequency is observable in Vercel logs, but I did not read them). I also did not count existing orphan clients at Willow, so the practical blast radius to date is unknown.
findings.rationale: Confirmed, but materially narrower than the audit described, which is why I move it from P2 to P3. The ordering defect is real and exactly as stated: the clients INSERT at :669 and the existing-client sms_consent UPDATE at :624 both commit before the appointments INSERT at :770, and every failure branch at :793-826 returns without compensating. There is no transaction and no cleanup path anywhere in the 1087-line action. What the audit missed is that the action already re-verifies the slot at :488-509 and returns before touching clients, so the obvious abuse path (deliberately submitting an occupied slot to farm client rows) is closed. The surviving exposure is a genuine but narrow TOCTOU race between that slot check and the insert (23P01 from the actual-overlap GiST exclusion, or HB001 from migration 0152's buffer trigger) plus any other database error on the appointments insert. Impact is data hygiene rather than integrity or authorization: an orphan client row in the studio directory that also permanently occupies its (studio_id, normalized_email) unique-index slot, and possibly an sms_consent_at stamp for a booking that never happened. That consent stamp reflects genuine consent (the visitor ticked the box and the submitted phone digits had to match the stored phone), so it is misleading provenance rather than fabricated consent. The post-commit side effects the audit worried about (marketing consent, appointment_audit, emails) are correctly sequenced after success.
findings.remediation_dependency: The correct fix is a single SECURITY DEFINER public-booking command that in one transaction validates the slot, creates-or-reuses the client, records consent evidence, inserts the appointment and writes the audit row, with email/SMS dispatched from an outbox after commit - a substantial rewrite of a 1087-line action that should not be done piecemeal. A cheap interim mitigation is a compensating delete of the just-created client when the appointment insert fails and that client has no other appointments and no sessions.
findings.rollout_required: Migration-first if implemented as a DB command (new function, service-role-only execute, called by the existing server action). Needs fault-injection tests forcing 23P01/HB001 that assert zero durable client/consent side effects, plus a one-off reconciliation query listing clients with no appointments and no sessions so any existing orphans can be reviewed rather than silently deleted.
findings.rollback_strategy: forward-fix via a new migration; applied migrations are never edited
findings.acceptance_evidence: Source-stated acceptance criteria (Hone_Independent_Audit_2026-07-27.md): Fault-injection and race tests assert zero durable side effects on every rejected submit.

findings.current_title: Public booking reuses an existing client from an unverified email, permitting nuisance bookings attributed to a real client and an existing-client enumeration oracle
findings.affected_roles: Existing clients of any publicly bookable studio (Willow's clients today); the studio owner (Chloe) absorbs the calendar and support cost. Anonymous/unauthenticated attacker; no account needed.
findings.exact_current_source: app/book/[slug]/actions.ts:534-540 (existing-client lookup by exact normalized_email, active only, via the service-role admin client - no proof of control of the address anywhere in the flow), :574-576 (clientType='existing' with no active match returns EXISTING_CLIENT_NO_MATCH_ERROR, defined at :94-95 - a response distinguishable from the success path, which is the enumeration oracle), :577-600 (existing client reused: clientId/clientName/clientPhone taken from the stored row; submitted name and phone are deliberately NOT written back - the P0 hardening comment at :578-599), :615-645 (the one remaining mutation on someone else's record: sms_consent_at + sms_consent_source, gated on the checkbox AND sms_opted_out_at IS NULL AND sms_consent_at IS NULL AND normalized submitted phone digits === stored phone digits), :484-486 (clientType='new' is forced onto a consultation service), :770-792 (appointment inserted with status 'confirmed' immediately - no confirmation step), :332-334 (PublicBookResult returns only { ok, appointmentId } - no client data echoed back), :833-846 (owner new_booking notification, so the abuse is detectable); lib/rate-limit:228-259 (limitPublicBooking: 5/10min per hashed IP+slug, 3/hour per hashed email+slug, and `return { allowed: true }; // fail open` at :255-258 when the limiter backend is unavailable, plus `if (!ipLimiter || !emailLimiter) return { allowed: true }` at :233-235 when it is unconfigured)
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: None queried directly. Hosted facts supplied establish Willow is the live studio with real client and payment activity; the public booking surface is a core deployed feature and the readiness gate at actions.ts:455-464 determines whether /book/<slug> accepts submissions.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: Not executed - no abuse test was run against production or a local instance. Everything above is traced from the deployed action source and the rate-limiter implementation. The audit's own note that abuse tests are needed still stands.
findings.missing_evidence: I did not confirm from a hosted read that Willow's public booking page currently passes the readiness gate (loadPublicReadiness at :455-464), so "live and bookable today" rests on documented product state rather than a live probe. The rate-limiter question is NOT open: F-OPS-001 establishes that missing Upstash configuration is caught by a production build gate, so the fail-open path requires a live Upstash/Redis outage rather than a config mistake. What remains unproven is limiter behaviour during such an outage, which no test exercises.
findings.rationale: Confirmed, and the only finding in this batch I hold at the audit's P2. It is reachable today by any anonymous internet user against a live studio's public booking page, needing only the studio slug, a client email and a free slot. Two distinct harms follow, and the second is the one the audit under-weighted. (1) Nuisance/impersonation: bookings are created with status 'confirmed' immediately, attached to a real client's profile, consuming real calendar capacity; there is no confirmation step and no ownership proof. (2) Enumeration: submitting clientType='existing' returns a distinguishable EXISTING_CLIENT_NO_MATCH_ERROR for a non-client versus a successful booking for a client, making the surface an oracle for "is this email address a client of this electrolysis studio" - health-adjacent information for a hair-removal practice. Each positive probe costs the attacker a real appointment, and the per-email limit (3/hour) does not constrain probing DISTINCT emails; only the 5/10min per-IP limit does, and that limiter both fails open on backend error and is a no-op if unconfigured. Real mitigations that reduce this below the audit's framing: the submitted name and phone are never written back to the stored client record (an earlier P0 fix), the response body leaks no client data, the consent mutation requires the attacker to already know the client's stored phone number, new clients are forced onto a consultation service, and the owner receives a new_booking notification. So the audit's "can mutate selected consent fields" is largely closed; impersonation and enumeration are not.
findings.remediation_dependency: Requires an explicit product decision on booking friction before any code. In increasing friction: (a) make the existing-client failure response indistinguishable from the new-client path so the oracle closes; (b) require an emailed magic-link confirmation before an existing-client booking becomes 'confirmed' (book as pending until the link is followed); (c) anti-abuse scoring. (a) is cheap and closes the enumeration channel alone. (b) closes impersonation but changes the client experience and must be validated with Chloe. Independently worth hardening: limitPublicBooking failing open at lib/rate-limit:255-258, which means a limiter outage removes the only volume control.
findings.rollout_required: Code-only for the indistinguishable-response change. A pending-confirmation model would need an appointment status/expiry concept and therefore a migration plus a sweep job, and must be workflow-validated with Chloe before shipping. If the current posture is retained, it should be reclassified as an explicitly accepted risk with the controls (rate limits, owner notification, one-click cancel) and the disclosure written down - not left implicit.
findings.acceptance_evidence: Source-stated acceptance criteria (Hone_Independent_Audit_2026-07-27.md): Browser tests for known-email impersonation, repeated nuisance submissions, rate-limiter outage and confirmation expiry.

findings.current_title: Whole-session-copy provenance ledger cascades away: both source and target session FKs are ON DELETE CASCADE
findings.affected_roles: Studio members reviewing session provenance (Chloe) and any future audit/export consumer. Triggerable only by whoever can delete a sessions row - today an authenticated studio member via direct PostgREST DELETE, or the database owner/service_role.
findings.exact_current_source: supabase/migrations/0157_whole_session_copy_setup.sql:69-95 (create table public.session_copy_operations), specifically :70 (studio_id references public.studios(id) on delete cascade), :80-82 (constraint session_copy_operations_target_same_studio_fk foreign key (studio_id, target_session_id) references public.sessions (studio_id, id) ON DELETE CASCADE) and :83-85 (constraint session_copy_operations_source_same_studio_fk foreign key (studio_id, source_session_id) references public.sessions (studio_id, id) ON DELETE CASCADE); contrast :86-90 where the practitioner FK deliberately uses ON DELETE RESTRICT; :92 (unique (target_session_id, idempotency_key) - the at-most-once key, lost with the row); :101-120 (RLS enabled, members SELECT only; `revoke all ... from public, anon, authenticated` then `grant select to authenticated`). Repository-wide grep found NO application code path that hard-deletes a sessions row: no `.delete()` against sessions in app or lib, and the only session-scoped delete RPC is 0123 soft_delete_session_area (soft delete of an area, not the session).
findings.exact_hosted_evidence: Hosted facts supplied: migration max 0160, so 0157 is applied. Authoritative ACL fact supplied: `authenticated` still holds row DML on sessions (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) - documented limitation L18 - while anon is SELECT-only on all clinical tables, and anon/authenticated are NOLOGIN so only PostgREST (authenticator) and postgres can connect; PostgREST does expose DELETE. Documented prior state: session_copy_operations had 0 rows at post-deploy verification.
findings.behavioural_test_evidence: Not executed. Verified by reading the 0157 constraint definitions directly and by grepping the entire app/ and lib/ tree for a hard session delete (none found), establishing that the deletion trigger is not an application path today.
findings.missing_evidence: I did not query the hosted session_copy_operations row count as of today, so I cannot state how many provenance rows currently exist and are at risk (it was 0 at deploy). I also did not verify whether the RLS policy on sessions actually permits a studio member's direct PostgREST DELETE to succeed - the grant exists per the supplied ACL facts, but the effective row-level DELETE policy on sessions was not read, and that determines whether the browser-reachable deletion path is real or only theoretical.
findings.rationale: Confirmed exactly at the schema level: both session references cascade, and the contrast with the practitioner FK on the very next lines (ON DELETE RESTRICT) shows the cascade was a deliberate choice for sessions rather than an oversight of the pattern. Deleting the SOURCE session erases the provenance of a destination record that still exists - that is the real defect - and it also destroys the (target_session_id, idempotency_key) row that makes the copy at-most-once. Deleting the target matters less because the copied rows go with it. I rate this P3, not P2, on reachability and current exposure. No application surface hard-deletes a session anywhere in the tree (charting uses soft deletes) and no retention or administrative deletion path exists yet, so the audit's stated scenario describes a path that has not been built. The one live route is a studio member issuing a raw PostgREST DELETE on sessions, which the supplied ACL facts confirm authenticated still holds (L18) - a deliberate, separately tracked limitation. Exposure today is also minimal because the ledger was verified at 0 rows after deployment; but whole-session copy is LIVE, so rows will accumulate from now on and the cheap-fix window closes on its own.
findings.remediation_dependency: Depends on the retention/legal-hold model being decided first - the right target (RESTRICT vs SET NULL vs tombstone) follows from whether a session is ever genuinely destroyed. It also interacts with L18: if authenticated loses direct DELETE on sessions as part of the L18 remediation (26 app call sites moved to narrow commands, then revoke), the only remaining deletion actor becomes owner/service_role, and a RESTRICT would then correctly force an explicit decision instead of silent erasure. Sequencing L18 first is cheaper than doing both.
findings.rollout_required: Forward-only migration altering the two FK constraints (drop + recreate as SET NULL on nullable columns, or RESTRICT), plus denormalised durable columns so a surviving row stays interpretable without the FK target - the table already stores source_fingerprint, copied_block_count and created_block_ids, so it mainly needs a human-readable source descriptor and the source session date. Because the ledger is currently empty or near-empty this can be done now with no backfill risk; the same change later would require deciding what to do with rows whose parents are already gone. Add a DB test that deletes the source session and asserts the provenance row survives and stays interpretable.
findings.rollback_strategy: forward-fix via a new migration; applied migrations are never edited
findings.acceptance_evidence: Source-stated acceptance criteria (Hone_Independent_Audit_2026-07-27.md): DB test deletes/archives source/target and verifies provenance remains interpretable.
